name: Normal Queue
html:
Welcome back, dear reader. So, did you understand the INTRODUCTION TO QUEUES video? This is the new data structure that we are going to use for some questions now and we will be looking at every aspect of this data structure. So, what is this question all about?

Important Links :Question Video, Solution Video

Watch video Problem Discussion :

We have to build a queue of ours with the same features and implementations of the queue data structure that we have studied in the INTRODUCTION TO QUEUES video. We recommend you watch the question video to understand the question completely and get a better idea of what exactly we need to do.

Watch video Approach :

Dear reader, we strongly recommend you watch the INTRODUCTION TO QUEUES video as the fundamentals of the queue data structure are taught in that video and we are going to use those concepts directly here. Still, let us revise the queue data structure in-short

The Queue Data Structure:
  1. The queue data structure is a dynamic data structure which is based on the FIFO principle i.e. first-in-first-out principle. The element that is entered first into the queue is the element that will get removed from the queue first whenever we try to remove elements from it. It is almost the opposite of the stack data structure which is based on the LIFO principle i.e. Last-in-first-out.
  2. The elements are entered in the queue from the rear end or in other words the elements are always inserted at the back of the queue.
  3. The elements are always removed from the front of the queue.
  4. Both insertion and deletion of an element from the queue take O(1) time.

Now, let us see what all is given to us in the question and what all we need to implement, and how we will implement it.

Given:

  1. We are given a CustomQueue class with three data members. But the CustomQueue class has a parameter called "cap", which stands for capacity.
  2. This means that we are making a queue of a fixed capacity. Now, why is that so? We know that a queue is a dynamic data structure. So, why are we limiting its capacity? Let's just say, we have a lot to implement and learn in this question. So, adding the feature of dynamic capacity will be done in the next question. For now, we will focus on making a queue of a fixed size.
  3. There are three data members inside this class:
    • The Data Array: that will contain all the data of the queue.
    • The Front Variable: that will always remain at the first element of the queue to ease the methods that we are going to apply.
    • The Size Variable: that will tell us the current size of the queue i.e. the total number of elements present in the queue at a given time.

Now that we know completely about all the things we needed to know before starting the process, let's now dive into it:

Building a Queue:

Now we will try to build a queue with all the knowledge of the queue that we have. We will implement all the methods as per the working of the queue data structure.

Building a Linear Queue:

Wait! What? A linear queue? What do we mean by this? You will come to know why we are calling this a linear queue later in this article. As we know the queue data structure works in a FIFO (first-in-first-out) fashion. So, we add the data at the end of the queue every time and we remove the data from its front. Have a look at the figure shown below where we are trying to add some elements in the queue. Notice that they are always added at the end of the queue.

We keep on adding the data in the queue and data gets added at the last of the queue. Now, if we try to add any more elements to the queue we will not be able to add those elements as the queue is full. The condition for the queue to be full is when this array "data" becomes full. So, the condition is size=data.length.

How to add?

So, we are adding the values into the queue always at the rear end. Let us call the index at which value is inserted as rear and rear=front +size. For instance, initially the front is at 0 and the size is also 0. So, rear=front+size=0+0=0, and we add the value 10 at data[rear]. Then after adding a value, the size becomes 1. So, the next value is added at rear=front+size=0+1=1. So, data[rear]=data[1]=20. We can continue inserting like this.

Similarly, the removal of elements from the queue is shown below:

How to remove?

We always remove the first element from the queue. The elements shown in purple indicate that they are not a part of the queue anymore. For instance, we remove 10 from the queue, not by shifting the elements, just by moving front to the next index (and decrementing the size value by 1) indicating that the queue now starts from index 1 and any element before index=1is not a part of the queue. When size=0, there is no element left in the queue and we cannot dequeue (remove) any element from the queue. So, if we try to remove any element after this, we will print "queue underflow".

Did you notice anything strange in this behavior of queue? Hint: look at (fig-3) the last array, when the queue is empty. We will talk about this in a short while.

The Size Method:

This method returns the size or the number of elements present in a queue at a particular time. We have nothing to do with this method as whenever we add an element to the queue, we increment the size data member of the queue class. So, we just have to "return size" in this method.

The Peek Method:

The peek method returns the value at the front of the queue. So, there is nothing special to do in this function also. We just have to return data[front]

The Display Method:

We have to display all the elements of a queue in this method. So, we will go from the front to the size of the queue and display all the elements.

You may refer to the solution video to clear your doubts regarding this method and understand the code written below completely.

Watch video

Now that we know every method, let us code these methods and see whether our implementation is perfect or not.

Java Code For Linear Queue: import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { public static class CustomQueue { int[] data; int front; int size; public CustomQueue(int cap) { data = new int[cap]; front = 0; size = 0; } int size() { return size; } void display() { for(int i = front; i < size; i++){ System.out.print(data[i] + " "); } System.out.println(); } void add(int val) { if(size == data.length){ //if queue is already full System.out.println("Queue overflow"); } else { int rear=front+size; data[rear]=val; size++; //as a new values is added } } int remove() { if(size == 0){ //if queue is already empty System.out.println("Queue underflow"); return -1; } else { int val = data[front]; front++; //queue will be from front to size size--; //as a value is removed return val; } } int peek() { if(size == 0){ //if queue is empty System.out.println("Queue underflow"); return -1; } else { int val = data[front]; return val; } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); CustomQueue qu = new CustomQueue(n); String str = br.readLine(); while(str.equals("quit") == false){ if(str.startsWith("add")){ int val = Integer.parseInt(str.split(" ")[1]); qu.add(val); } else if(str.startsWith("remove")){ int val = qu.remove(); if(val != -1){ System.out.println(val); } } else if(str.startsWith("peek")){ int val = qu.peek(); if(val != -1){ System.out.println(val); } } else if(str.startsWith("size")){ System.out.println(qu.size()); } else if(str.startsWith("display")){ qu.display(); } str = br.readLine(); } } }
java; true";

So, this is the code for a linear queue. Again, what is a linear queue? Why are we calling this queue a linear queue? We suggest you think about the above code and watch the question video once again and try to analyze whether this code does all that we want or not?

Watch video Need for a Circular Queue:

Now you will understand the difference between a linear and a circular queue and why we called our previous implementation a linear queue. Let us take the last stage of the queue as shown in fig-2

The size of the queue is 0 as we have removed all the elements from the queue. Still, we can not enter any value into the queue as the front became 5 when we removed the last value and also rear=front+size=5+0=5, which is also an invalid position to enter a value into the queue.

Similarly, look at the diagram shown below:

We removed the first two elements from the queue. So, only three elements inside the array are now a part of the queue. Now, if we want to insert an element into the queue, it can be inserted at the rear position only. Now, rear=front+size=2+3=5, which is out of the bound for the array. So, even if 2 spaces were vacant in that array i.e. 2 spaces were available which were not a part of the queue, still, we could not insert our elements there.

So, you saw, in the first case, when we had the entire array vacant then also, we were not able to enter any values into it and we were not able to enter the values into the queue even if certain places (not the entire array) were vacant. So, what is the solution to this? Have a look at the diagram given below:

We want our queue to show a circular behavior like this to utilize the space available. So, this can be implemented easily, using a modulus operator. I hope you now got why we were calling our previous implementation a linear queue and this a circular queue.

Building Circular Queue:

Enqueue (Add) : While adding the values into the queue, we were calculating the rear as rear=front+size. Now, we will calculate rear as rear=(front+size)%data.length. This will help us achieve a circular implementation of the queue. (See fig-6). This is because the mod operator always works in a circular fashion. It cycles through its set of values again and again.

Dequeue (Remove): While removing the values, we will not just move front forward by doing front++. Rather, we will do: front=(front+1)%data.length. This will help achieve the circular implementation (See fig-7).

Display: While displaying the queue also, we will display it from the front. So, we will again increment the front as shown above i.e. front=(front+1)%data. length

The Size Method: This method will remain the same as we just have to return the size of the queue. We increment the size value while entering an element into the queue and we decrement it while removing an element from it. So, we do not have to handle anything in this method and it will be the same as the previous size method of the linear queue.

The Peek Method: The peek method returns the first element of the queue. So, we will simply return data[front] and this method also remains the same in both cases.

You may refer to the SOLUTION VIDEO to understand the above-explained procedure completely and also understand the code for the circular queue given below:

Watch video Java Code For Circular Queue: import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { public static class CustomQueue { int[] data; int front; int size; public CustomQueue(int cap) { data = new int[cap]; front = 0; size = 0; } int size() { return size; } void display() { for(int i = 0; i < size; i++){ int idx = (front + i) % data.length; System.out.print(data[idx] + " "); } System.out.println(); } void add(int val) { if(size == data.length){ System.out.println("Queue overflow"); } else { int idx = (front + size) % data.length; data[idx] = val; size++; } } int remove() { if(size == 0){ System.out.println("Queue underflow"); return -1; } else { int val = data[front]; front = (front + 1) % data.length; size--; return val; } } int peek() { if(size == 0){ System.out.println("Queue underflow"); return -1; } else { int val = data[front]; return val; } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); CustomQueue qu = new CustomQueue(n); String str = br.readLine(); while(str.equals("quit") == false){ if(str.startsWith("add")){ int val = Integer.parseInt(str.split(" ")[1]); qu.add(val); } else if(str.startsWith("remove")){ int val = qu.remove(); if(val != -1){ System.out.println(val); } } else if(str.startsWith("peek")){ int val = qu.peek(); if(val != -1){ System.out.println(val); } } else if(str.startsWith("size")){ System.out.println(qu.size()); } else if(str.startsWith("display")){ qu.display(); } str = br.readLine(); } } }
java; true";

So dear reader, we hope that you understood in-depth, the implementation of queue data structure. If you still have any doubts regarding the procedure that we follow or the code, you may refer to the complete solution video to clear all your doubts.

Watch video Analysis Time Complexity :

Add: We always add the element at the last index in the queue but for that, we do not traverse the array. We directly access the last index. So, the time complexity is O(1).

Remove: We always remove the first element from the queue and we do not traverse the queue at all. So, the time complexity will be O(1).

Peek: We just have to return data[front], so the time complexity is O(1).

Size: We just have to return the size of the queue. So, the time complexity is O(1).

Display: For this, we have to traverse the entire array (queue) to print all the values. So, the time complexity is O(n).

SPACE COMPLEXITY :

Let us talk about space complexity first. We have not used any extra data structure to implement any of the above-mentioned methods. So, the space complexity for all these methods is O(1).

Suggestions:

Here are some suggestions from our side that you do not want to miss:

  1. We suggest you watch the solution video once again and also go through the article once more to understand the in-depth difference between the two types of queues (linear and circular) we used here.
  2. The code is entirely logical as always. If you understand the working of the queue completely, you can easily convert your thoughts into code. We suggest you code this problem once more without taking any help. This will give you immense confidence and comfort with the queue data structure.
